Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ be open. Write $\Omega^k(U;\mathbb C)$ for smooth
complex-valued $k$-forms. For increasing multi-indices
$I=(i_1<\cdots<i_p)$ and $J=(j_1<\cdots<j_q)$, write
$dz^I=dz_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dz_{i_p}$ and
$d\bar z^J=d\bar z_{j_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge d\bar z_{j_q}$. The invertible
change of cotangent basis
$dz_j=dx_j+i\,dy_j$, $d\bar z_j=dx_j-i\,dy_j$ gives the direct sum
decomposition

$$\Omega^k(U;\mathbb C)=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}\Omega^{p,q}(U),\qquad \Omega^{p,q}(U)=\left\{\sum_{I,J}a_{I,J}(z)\,dz^I\wedge d\bar z^J:a_{I,J}\in C^\infty(U;\mathbb C)\right\},$$

where $0\le p,q\le n$ and every sum is finite. On a $(p,q)$ form
$\eta=\sum_{I,J}a_{I,J}dz^I\wedge d\bar z^J$, define

$$\partial\eta=\sum_{I,J,j}(\partial_{z_j}a_{I,J})\,dz_j\wedge dz^I\wedge d\bar z^J,\qquad \bar\partial\eta=\sum_{I,J,j}(\partial_{\bar z_j}a_{I,J})\,d\bar z_j\wedge dz^I\wedge d\bar z^J.$$

Repeated differentials vanish by alternation; components outside the range
$0\le p,q\le n$ are zero. These operators are the components of $d$ of
bidegrees $(p+1,q)$ and $(p,q+1)$.

Assume AC. Let $n\ge1$, let $P=\prod_{j=1}^n D_j$ and
$P'=\prod_{j=1}^n D'_j$ be finite open coordinate polydiscs such that each
closed coordinate disc $\overline{D'_j}$ is a compact subset of $D_j$. Let
$0\le p\le n$ and $1\le q\le n$, and let $\eta\in\Omega^{p,q}(P)$ be a
smooth form with $\bar\partial\eta=0$. Then there is a smooth
$\psi\in\Omega^{p,q-1}(P')$ such that
$$\bar\partial\psi=\eta|_{P'}.$$

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb C$ be of
class $C^1$ in the real coordinates
([[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], applied to the real
and imaginary parts of $f$ on $U$ read as an open subset of $\mathbb R^{2m}$).
Let $a\in U$. The following are equivalent.

1. $f$ is complex differentiable at $a$.
2. $f$ is real totally differentiable at $a$ and its real total derivative
   $Df(a)$ is $\mathbb C$-linear.
3. $f$ is real totally differentiable at $a$ and
   $\partial_{\bar z_k}f(a)=0$ for every $k<m$ — the several-variable
   Cauchy–Riemann system.

The $C^1$ hypothesis is used **only** to pass from the Cauchy–Riemann system to
real total differentiability; the implications from 1 to 2 and between 2 and 3
hold at any point with no regularity beyond what each condition states.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be a smooth manifold
([[def-smooth-manifold]]), let
$\mathcal A=\mathcal C_M^\infty$ be its sheaf of real-valued smooth functions,
and let $\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of $\mathcal A$-modules. Then for every open
$U\subseteq M$ and every $q>0$,
$$H^q(U,\mathcal F|_U)=0.$$
The Axiom of Choice supplies injective resolutions for module sheaves and for
abelian-sheaf cohomology. Its consequences $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and DC supply,
respectively, the partitions of unity and the acyclic-resolution comparison
used below; no stronger choice principle is used.

Assume the Axiom of Dependent Choice.

Let $I$ be a supplied injective resolution datum on a class $\mathcal D$, let
$F:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B$ be an additive left exact functor, and let
$$0\to A\to J^0\to J^1\to J^2\to\cdots$$
be an $F$-acyclic resolution of $A$ relative to $I$. Assume moreover that
$A\in\mathcal D$ and that, for $Z^0:=A$ and
$$0\to Z^q\to J^q\to Z^{q+1}\to0\qquad(q\ge0),$$
each $Z^q$ lies in $\mathcal D$. Then for every $n\ge 0$ there is a canonical
isomorphism
$$R_I^nF(A)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }H^n(F(J^\bullet_{\mathrm{del}})).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix a topological space $X$, let
$$\Gamma(X,-):\mathrm{Ab}(X)\to\mathbf{Ab}$$
be the additive left exact global-sections functor
([[def-global-sections-functor-sheaves]]), and let $I$ be the supplied
functorial injective resolution datum on $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ of
[[thm-abelian-sheaves-have-enough-injectives]]: it assigns to every abelian
sheaf $\mathcal F$ one specific injective resolution
$0\to\mathcal F\to I^\bullet(\mathcal F)$
([[def-right-derived-object-relative-to-injective-resolution-data]]).

For every $q\ge0$ and every abelian sheaf $\mathcal F$ on $X$ define the
**$q$-th sheaf cohomology group of $\mathcal F$** to be the right derived
object of $\Gamma(X,-)$ relative to $I$:
$$H^q(X,\mathcal F):=R_I^q\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)=H^q\bigl(\Gamma(X,I^\bullet(\mathcal F)_{\mathrm{del}})\bigr),$$
the cohomology object of the complex
$\Gamma(X,I^0(\mathcal F))\to\Gamma(X,I^1(\mathcal F))\to\cdots$ of abelian
groups obtained from the deleted resolution
([[def-deleted-resolution]], [[def-cohomology-object-of-a-cochain-complex]]).
We also set $H^q(X,\mathcal F):=0$ for $q<0$.

Because $I$ is a fixed supplied datum, the group $H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ is a
specific group for each pair $(X,\mathcal F)$, and for a morphism
$\varphi:\mathcal F\to\mathcal G$ of abelian sheaves we write
$H^q(X,\varphi):=R_I^q\Gamma(X,\varphi)$ for the induced map; it is the map on
cohomology induced by $\Gamma(X,-)$ applied to the cochain maps supplied with
the datum, and it is additive in $\varphi$.

If $J$ is another supplied injective resolution datum on $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ then
$R_I^q\Gamma(X,-)$ and $R_J^q\Gamma(X,-)$ are naturally isomorphic, so the
$H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ computed from $J$ agree with the ones above up to a
canonical natural isomorphism; the Axiom of Dependent Choice needed for that
comparison follows from AC
([[thm-right-derived-functors-from-two-supplied-injective-resolution-data-are-naturally-isomorphic]],
[[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]). The notation
$H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ therefore does not depend on the datum used, up to this
canonical isomorphism, and we call $q$ the **cohomological degree**.

Assume the Axiom of Choice (AC). Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C^n$
be a domain, and suppose that $\Omega$ is Hartogs pseudoconvex
([[def-plurisubharmonic-exhaustion-and-hartogs-pseudoconvexity]]). Let
$1\le q\le n$.

1. **(Smooth vanishing.)** Every smooth $\bar\partial$-closed $(0,q)$-form
   $\eta\in\Omega^{0,q}(\Omega)$ ([[def-bigraded-complex-differential-forms]])
   is exact in the Dolbeault complex: there is
   $\zeta\in\Omega^{0,q-1}(\Omega)$ with $\bar\partial\zeta=\eta$.
   Consequently $H^{0,q}_{\bar\partial}(\Omega)=0$
   ([[def-dolbeault-cohomology-domain]]).

2. **(Weighted $L^2$ exactness under finite energy.)** Let
   $\varphi\in C^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ be strictly plurisubharmonic on $\Omega$
   ([[def-levi-form-and-strict-plurisubharmonicity]]); for $a\in\Omega$ let
   $\lambda_1(a)\le\cdots\le\lambda_n(a)$ be the eigenvalues of the Hermitian
   matrix $(\varphi_{j\bar k}(a))$ and put
   $w(a):=\lambda_1(a)+\cdots+\lambda_q(a)>0$. If
   $f\in\operatorname{Dom}\bar\partial_q$ satisfies $\bar\partial_qf=0$ and
   $$E(f):=\int_\Omega|f|^2w^{-1}e^{-\varphi}\,dV<+\infty,$$
   then there is $u\in\operatorname{Dom}\bar\partial_{q-1}$ with
   $\bar\partial_{q-1}u=f$ and $\|u\|_\varphi^2\le E(f)$.

No boundary regularity of the primitives is claimed, and the statement is
asserted for $1\le q\le n$ only.

derivations.claim: On each coordinate polydisc in $\Omega$, [F2] says the sequence of sheaves $0\to\mathcal O_\Omega\to\mathcal A^{0,0}\xrightarrow{\bar\partial}\mathcal A^{0,1}\xrightarrow{\bar\partial}\cdots$ is exact in positive degree. Its degree-zero kernel is exactly $\mathcal O_\Omega$: a smooth function in that kernel has all $\bar z$-derivatives zero and is holomorphic by [F3]. Thus it is an exact sheaf resolution on $\Omega$.

Each resolution term is a sheaf of modules over smooth functions and is $\Gamma(\Omega,-)$-acyclic by [F4]. The acyclic-resolution theorem [F5] therefore identifies $H^q(\Omega,\mathcal O_\Omega)$ with the cohomology in degree $q$ of the global smooth Dolbeault complex.

For $1\le q\le m$, [F6] makes every closed global smooth $(0,q)$-form exact, so the degree-$q$ cohomology in step 2.1 is zero. For $q>m$, the complex has no $(0,q)$-forms on an $m$-dimensional complex manifold, so its degree-$q$ cohomology is zero as well. Hence $H^q(\Omega,\mathcal O_\Omega)=0$ for every $q>0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional complex manifold and let $\mathcal O_M$ be its sheaf of holomorphic functions. For every open $U\subseteq M$ and every finite tuple $f_1,\ldots,f_q\in\mathcal O_M(U)$, the relation sheaf
$$
\ker\!\left(\mathcal O_U^{\oplus q}\longrightarrow\mathcal O_U,\quad(a_1,\ldots,a_q)\longmapsto\sum_{j=1}^q a_jf_j\right)
$$
is locally of finite type: every point has a neighborhood on which one finite family of relation sections generates the relation stalk at every point. Consequently $\mathcal O_M$ is coherent. Coherent $\mathcal O_M$-module sheaves are closed under kernels, cokernels, and finite extensions. For every coherent $\mathcal O_M$-module $\mathcal F$, point $x\in M$, and finite integer $\ell\ge0$, there are a chart neighborhood $W$ of $x$ and finite ranks $p_0,\ldots,p_\ell$ for which
$$
\mathcal O_W^{\oplus p_\ell}\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow\mathcal O_W^{\oplus p_0}\longrightarrow\mathcal F|_W\longrightarrow0
$$
is exact at $\mathcal F|_W$ and at every free term except the leftmost one. No exactness at the leftmost free term and no global analytic free resolution are asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Choice (AC) and the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C^n$, $n\ge1$, be a domain and let $u:\Omega\to\mathbb R$
be a continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion, that is, $u$ is continuous and
plurisubharmonic and every sublevel set $\{z\in\Omega:u(z)\le c\}$,
$c\in\mathbb R$, is a compact subset of $\Omega$.

Then there exist a function $S\in C^\infty(\Omega)$ and a strictly increasing
sequence $c_1<c_2<\cdots$ with $c_k\to+\infty$ such that, writing
$\Omega_k:=\{z\in\Omega:S(z)<c_k\}$:

1. $S$ is strictly plurisubharmonic on $\Omega$, $S>u$ on $\Omega$, and $S$ is
   again an exhaustion of $\Omega$, that is, $\{z\in\Omega:S(z)\le c\}$ is a
   compact subset of $\Omega$ for every real $c$;
2. every $c_k$ is a regular value of $S$, and
   $\partial\Omega_k=\{z\in\Omega:S(z)=c_k\}$ is a nonempty $C^\infty$
   hypersurface of $\Omega$;
3. $\overline{\Omega_k}\subseteq\Omega_{k+1}$ and
   $\bigcup_{k\ge1}\Omega_k=\Omega$, so every $\overline{\Omega_k}$ is a compact
   subset of $\Omega$;
4. (strong pseudoconvexity) for every $k$, every $p\in\partial\Omega_k$ and
   every $v\in\mathbb C^n\setminus\{0\}$ with
   $$\sum_{j<n}\frac{\partial S}{\partial z_j}(p)\,v_j=0$$
   one has $\mathcal L_S(p;v)>0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb C^n$, $n\ge1$, be a bounded domain with a smooth plurisubharmonic exhaustion $S$. Then $\Omega$ is Hartogs pseudoconvex: $-\log\delta_\Omega$ is plurisubharmonic, where $\delta_\Omega$ is the equal-radius polydisc boundary function.

Assume full AC. Let $m\ge1$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ be a Hartogs-pseudoconvex domain. Let $\mathcal O_\Omega$ be its sheaf of holomorphic functions. Then the derived sheaf cohomology satisfies $H^q(\Omega,\mathcal O_\Omega)=0$ for every integer $q>0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice (AC). Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C^n$
be a domain, and suppose that $\Omega$ is Hartogs pseudoconvex
([[def-plurisubharmonic-exhaustion-and-hartogs-pseudoconvexity]]). Let
$1\le q\le n$.

1. **(Smooth vanishing.)** Every smooth $\bar\partial$-closed $(0,q)$-form
   $\eta\in\Omega^{0,q}(\Omega)$ ([[def-bigraded-complex-differential-forms]])
   is exact in the Dolbeault complex: there is
   $\zeta\in\Omega^{0,q-1}(\Omega)$ with $\bar\partial\zeta=\eta$.
   Consequently $H^{0,q}_{\bar\partial}(\Omega)=0$
   ([[def-dolbeault-cohomology-domain]]).

2. **(Weighted $L^2$ exactness under finite energy.)** Let
   $\varphi\in C^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ be strictly plurisubharmonic on $\Omega$
   ([[def-levi-form-and-strict-plurisubharmonicity]]); for $a\in\Omega$ let
   $\lambda_1(a)\le\cdots\le\lambda_n(a)$ be the eigenvalues of the Hermitian
   matrix $(\varphi_{j\bar k}(a))$ and put
   $w(a):=\lambda_1(a)+\cdots+\lambda_q(a)>0$. If
   $f\in\operatorname{Dom}\bar\partial_q$ satisfies $\bar\partial_qf=0$ and
   $$E(f):=\int_\Omega|f|^2w^{-1}e^{-\varphi}\,dV<+\infty,$$
   then there is $u\in\operatorname{Dom}\bar\partial_{q-1}$ with
   $\bar\partial_{q-1}u=f$ and $\|u\|_\varphi^2\le E(f)$.

No boundary regularity of the primitives is claimed, and the statement is
asserted for $1\le q\le n$ only.

Assume full AC. Let $m\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be a nonempty
open subset with its Euclidean metric, and let $\mathcal G$ be any sheaf of
abelian groups on $\Omega$. Then ordinary derived-functor sheaf cohomology
satisfies
$$H^q(\Omega,\mathcal G)=0\qquad\text{for every integer }q>m.$$
This is an ordinary cohomology bound for arbitrary sheaves; it is not a
compact-support cohomology assertion.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let
$$0\to\mathcal F'\to\mathcal F\to\mathcal F''\to0$$
be a short exact sequence of abelian sheaves on a topological space $X$, and let
$H^q(X,-)$ be sheaf cohomology computed from the supplied functorial injective
resolution datum $I$ on $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$
([[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]). Then there is a natural long
exact sequence
$$\cdots\to H^q(X,\mathcal F')\to H^q(X,\mathcal F)\to H^q(X,\mathcal F'')\xrightarrow{\partial^q}H^{q+1}(X,\mathcal F')\to H^{q+1}(X,\mathcal F)\to\cdots,$$
natural in the short exact sequence and independent of the choice of injective
resolutions used to assemble it.

The derived categories and right derived functor here are taken under the
standing smallness or supplied cofinal-denominator hypothesis of
[[def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category]].

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ be a domain. A function
$u:\Omega\to[-\infty,\infty)$ is **plurisubharmonic** when:

1. $u$ is upper semicontinuous;
2. on no connected component of $\Omega$ is $u$ identically $-\infty$;
3. for every $a\in\Omega$ and every nonzero $v\in\mathbb C^m$, the function
   $$u_{a,v}(\lambda):=u(a+\lambda v)$$
   is subharmonic or identically $-\infty$ on each connected component of
   $$\{\lambda\in\mathbb C: a+\lambda v\in\Omega\}.$$

Fix an integer $m\ge1$. In this Definition, use one-based aliases for the canonical coordinates of
[[rem-complex-euclidean-space-dictionary]]: for $1\le j\le m$, the symbols
$z_j$ and $v_j$ denote the canonical coordinate and vector component with
index $j-1$. The derivatives $\partial_{z_j}$ and
$\partial_{\overline z_j}$ denote the corresponding canonical Wirtinger
operators of [[def-wirtinger-operators-in-several-complex-variables]] with
index $j-1$; all derivatives below use these aliases.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ be open and let $u\in C^2(\Omega,\mathbb R)$.
For $a\in\Omega$ and $v\in\mathbb C^m$, the **Levi form** of $u$ at $a$ in the
direction $v$ is

$$\mathcal L_u(a;v):=\sum_{j=1}^m\sum_{k=1}^m \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial z_j\partial\overline z_k}(a)\,v_j\overline{v_k}.$$

The function $u$ is **strictly plurisubharmonic** when

$$\mathcal L_u(a;v)>0\qquad\text{for every }a\in\Omega\text{ and every }v\ne0.$$

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ be open and let $u\in C^2(\Omega,\mathbb R)$.
Then $u$ is plurisubharmonic on $\Omega$ if and only if

$$\mathcal L_u(a;v)\ge0\qquad\text{for every }a\in\Omega\text{ and every }v\in\mathbb C^m.$$

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ be a domain.

1. If $u_1,\dots,u_N$ are plurisubharmonic on $\Omega$ and
   $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_N\ge0$, then
   $$\alpha_1u_1+\cdots+\alpha_Nu_N$$
   is plurisubharmonic, with the zero-coefficient terms omitted.
2. If $u_1,\dots,u_N$ are plurisubharmonic on $\Omega$, then
   $$u(z)=\max\{u_1(z),\dots,u_N(z)\}$$
   is plurisubharmonic.
3. If $u:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ is plurisubharmonic and
   $\phi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is convex and nondecreasing, then
   $\phi\circ u$ is plurisubharmonic on $\Omega$.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ and $V\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ be domains, let
$F:\Omega\to V$ be holomorphic, and let $u\in C^2(V,\mathbb R)$ be
plurisubharmonic. Then $u\circ F$ is plurisubharmonic on $\Omega$.

derivations.claim: Choose the chart of $D_{i_0}$ and write $V$ in those coordinates. For each $D_i$, the function $\rho_{D_i}$ in [F6] is a smooth plurisubharmonic exhaustion of $D_i$; on $V$ it remains plurisubharmonic after composing with the holomorphic chart transition. The continuous function $\rho:=\max_{1\le i\le s}\rho_{D_i}$ is plurisubharmonic by [F6]. If a sequence in $V$ leaves every compact subset of $V$, it approaches the boundary of at least one of the finitely many $D_i$, and the corresponding $\rho_{D_i}$ tends to $+\infty$. Thus $\rho$ is an exhaustion of $V$.

Each connected component $V_\alpha$ is a bounded domain in the chart of $D_{i_0}$ and inherits the continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion $\rho$. Apply [F1] to obtain a smooth plurisubharmonic exhaustion on $V_\alpha$, then [F2] to conclude that $V_\alpha$ is Hartogs pseudoconvex. By [F3], $H^q(V_\alpha,\mathcal O)=0$ for $q>0$, hence $H^q(V_\alpha,\mathcal O^{p})=0$ for every finite rank $p$.

Restrict the assumed partial resolution to $V_\alpha$ and define $K_{-1}=\mathcal F|_{V_\alpha}$ and $K_j=\ker(\mathcal O_{V_\alpha}^{p_j}\to\mathcal O_{V_\alpha}^{p_{j-1}})$ for $1\le j\le2r$, with $K_0=\ker(\mathcal O_{V_\alpha}^{p_0}\to K_{-1})$. Exactness of the resolution through the penultimate free term gives short exact sequences $0\to K_j\to\mathcal O_{V_\alpha}^{p_j}\to K_{j-1}\to0$ for $0\le j\le2r$, where at $j=0$ the rightmost term is $K_{-1}$. By [A1] each $K_j$ is coherent, and by step 2.1 the middle free sheaf in each sequence is acyclic in positive degree.

The long exact sequence [F5] for each short exact sequence in step 3.1 therefore gives, for every $q>0$, isomorphisms $H^q(V_\alpha,K_{j-1})\cong H^{q+1}(V_\alpha,K_j)$ for $j=0,1,\ldots,2r$. Iterating yields $H^q(V_\alpha,\mathcal F)\cong H^{q+2r+1}(V_\alpha,K_{2r})$. The chart identifies $V_\alpha$ with an open subset of $\mathbb C^r\cong\mathbb R^{2r}$, so [F4] makes the last group zero because $q+2r+1>2r$.

The components of the open set $V$ are disjoint open subsets and are at most countable because the chart is second countable. Sheaves on their disjoint union are tuples of sheaves on the components; global sections are products, and products of abelian groups are exact under AC. Applying componentwise injective resolutions therefore gives $H^q(V,\mathcal F)=\prod_\alpha H^q(V_\alpha,\mathcal F)=0$ for $q>0$ by step 4.1.

Let $(X,\mathcal O_X)$ be a ringed space, so $X$ is a topological space and $\mathcal O_X$ is a sheaf of commutative rings. An $\mathcal O_X$-module sheaf $\mathcal F$ is **locally of finite type** if for every $x\in X$ there are an open neighborhood $U$ of $x$, a finite integer $r\ge0$, and sections $s_1,\ldots,s_r\in\mathcal F(U)$ such that their germs generate $\mathcal F_y$ as an $\mathcal O_{X,y}$-module for every $y\in U$.

For an open $V\subseteq X$, a finite integer $p\ge0$, and an $\mathcal O_X$-module morphism $\phi:\mathcal O_V^{\oplus p}\to\mathcal F|_V$, its **relation sheaf** is the kernel sheaf $\ker\phi$. The module sheaf $\mathcal F$ is **coherent** if it is locally of finite type and, for every such $V$, $p$, and $\phi$, the relation sheaf $\ker\phi$ is locally of finite type. Here $\mathcal O_V^{\oplus0}$ is the zero module sheaf.

In particular, for a finite tuple $f_1,\ldots,f_p\in\mathcal O_X(U)$, its holomorphic relation sheaf is the kernel of the morphism $\mathcal O_U^{\oplus p}\to\mathcal O_U$ that sends $(a_1,\ldots,a_p)$ to $\sum_{j=1}^p a_jf_j$. The structure sheaf is coherent when it is coherent as a module over itself. If $M$ is a complex manifold, an **analytic coherent module on $M$** means a coherent module sheaf over its sheaf $\mathcal O_M$ of holomorphic functions.

For every integer $m\ge1$, the holomorphic germ ring $\mathcal O_{m,0}$ is a
Noetherian commutative ring.

Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring, let $I\subset R$ be an ideal, let $M$
be a finite $R$-module, and let $N\subseteq M$ be a submodule. Then there exists
an integer $c\ge0$ such that
$$ I^nM\cap N = I^{n-c}(I^cM\cap N) $$
for every $n\ge c$.

The first clause below is choice-free; the second uses the published
Jacobson-radical unit criterion and therefore inherits its Axiom-of-Choice
boundary.

Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring, let $I\subset R$ be an ideal, and let
$M$ be a finite $R$-module. Put
$$ K:=\bigcap_{n\ge0} I^nM. $$
Then:

1. $K$ is exactly the set of elements $m\in M$ for which $(1-a)m=0$ for some
   $a\in I$;
2. if $I\subseteq J(R)$, then $K=0$.

Let $m\ge1$, let $a\in\mathbb C^m$, let $\rho$ be a polyradius and let
$f:\Delta_\rho(a)\to\mathbb C$ be holomorphic. Let $r$ be a polyradius with
$r_k<\rho_k$ for every $k<m$, and put $M=\sup_{\Gamma_r(a)}|f|$, the supremum
over the **distinguished boundary** only. Then for every multi-index $\alpha$

$$\bigl|\partial^\alpha_zf(a)\bigr|\ \le\ \alpha!\,M\prod_{k<m}r_k^{-\alpha_k}.$$

The bound uses no value of $f$ outside $\Gamma_r(a)$, which for $m\ge2$ is a
proper subset of the topological boundary of the closed polydisc.

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ be open, let each
$f_n:U\to\mathbb C$ be holomorphic, and suppose $f_n\to f$ locally uniformly on
$U$: every point of $U$ has a neighbourhood on which the convergence is uniform.
Then $f$ is holomorphic on $U$, and for every multi-index $\alpha$

$$\partial^\alpha_zf_n\longrightarrow\partial^\alpha_zf$$

locally uniformly on $U$.

Fix a natural number $m\ge1$. **Complex $m$-space** $\mathbb C^m$ is the set of

field $\mathbb C$ ([[def-vector-space]], [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]),

$$\Phi:\mathbb C^m\to\mathbb R^{2m},\qquad \Phi(z)=(x_0,y_0,x_1,y_1,\dots,x_{m-1},y_{m-1}).$$

is a **convergent Laurent series on $A(a;r,R)$** when, for every closed
subannulus

$$K_{\rho,\sigma}:=\{\,z\in\mathbb C:\rho\le|z-a|\le\sigma\,\}\subseteq A(a;r,R)$$

with $r<\rho\le\sigma<R$, both one-sided series on the right converge uniformly
on $K_{\rho,\sigma}$.

Its **sum** is the function $f:A(a;r,R)\to\mathbb C$ defined by that convergent
value at each point of the annulus, and the numbers $c_n$ are its **Laurent
coefficients**.

Let $f$ be holomorphic on the annulus $A(a;r,R)$ with $0\le r<R\le\infty$
([[def-complex-annulus]]). Then there are complex numbers $c_n$ indexed by
$n\in\mathbb Z$ such that

$$f(z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}c_n(z-a)^n$$

for every $z\in A(a;r,R)$, and the series converges locally uniformly on the
annulus. In other words, $f$ has a convergent Laurent series on $A(a;r,R)$
([[def-convergent-complex-laurent-series]]).

Let $\gamma$ be a fixed rectifiable contour. If continuous functions $f_n$ on its trace converge uniformly to a continuous $f$, then
$$\int_\gamma f_n(z)\,dz\longrightarrow\int_\gamma f(z)\,dz.$$

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ be open, let each
$f_n:U\to\mathbb C$ be holomorphic, and suppose $f_n\to f$ locally uniformly on
$U$: every point of $U$ has a neighbourhood on which the convergence is uniform.
Then $f$ is holomorphic on $U$, and for every multi-index $\alpha$

$$\partial^\alpha_zf_n\longrightarrow\partial^\alpha_zf$$

locally uniformly on $U$.

derivations.claim: By [F1], write $f(z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}c_nz^n$ on $\mathbb C^*$, with both one-sided series uniformly convergent on every compact subannulus. Fix $R>0$ and integrate the uniformly convergent series on the positively oriented circle $\gamma_R(t)=Re^{it}$ after multiplying by $z^{-n-1}$. By [F2], termwise integration is valid, and direct parametrization gives $(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_{\gamma_R}z^{k-n-1}\,dz=1$ for $k=n$ and $0$ otherwise. Thus $$ c_n=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{\gamma_R}f(z)z^{-n-1}\,dz $$ for every $n\in\mathbb Z$ and every $R>0$.
Put $M_R=\max_{|z|=R}|f(z)|$. The coefficient formula in step 1.1 and the circle length $2\pi R$ give $|c_n|\le M_RR^{-n}$ for $n\ge0$ and $|c_{-m}|\le M_RR^m$ for $m\ge1$.

Define $g(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}c_nz^n$. For any $S>0$, choose $R>S$; on $|z|\le S$ the terms satisfy $|c_nz^n|\le M_R(S/R)^n$ by step 2.1, so the series converges uniformly there. Its partial sums are polynomials, hence [F3] makes $g$ entire.

Define $h(w)=\sum_{j\ge0}c_{-(j+2)}w^j$. Given $S>0$, choose $0<R<1/S$; on $|w|\le S$ the terms satisfy $|c_{-(j+2)}w^j|\le M_RR^2(RS)^j$ by step 2.1, so this series also converges uniformly on every closed disk. Its partial sums are polynomials, and [F3] makes $h$ entire.

On each compact subannulus of $\mathbb C^*$, the Laurent series of [F1] is the sum of its nonnegative terms, its single $c_{-1}z^{-1}$ term, and its terms of degree at most $-2$. The first part is $g(z)$ by step 3.1, and the last part is $z^{-2}h(1/z)$ by step 3.2. Hence the displayed decomposition holds at every $z\ne0$.

If another pair of entire functions and scalar gave the same decomposition, their Taylor coefficients would give a Laurent expansion of $f$ on $\mathbb C^*$ with the same positive, $-1$, and lower negative powers. The contour formula in step 1.1 recovers each Laurent coefficient uniquely; therefore the scalar and all Taylor coefficients of both entire functions agree. The decomposition is unique.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional complex manifold and let $\mathcal O_M$ be its sheaf of holomorphic functions. For every open $U\subseteq M$ and every finite tuple $f_1,\ldots,f_q\in\mathcal O_M(U)$, the relation sheaf
$$
\ker\!\left(\mathcal O_U^{\oplus q}\longrightarrow\mathcal O_U,\quad(a_1,\ldots,a_q)\longmapsto\sum_{j=1}^q a_jf_j\right)
$$
is locally of finite type: every point has a neighborhood on which one finite family of relation sections generates the relation stalk at every point. Consequently $\mathcal O_M$ is coherent. Coherent $\mathcal O_M$-module sheaves are closed under kernels, cokernels, and finite extensions. For every coherent $\mathcal O_M$-module $\mathcal F$, point $x\in M$, and finite integer $\ell\ge0$, there are a chart neighborhood $W$ of $x$ and finite ranks $p_0,\ldots,p_\ell$ for which
$$
\mathcal O_W^{\oplus p_\ell}\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow\mathcal O_W^{\oplus p_0}\longrightarrow\mathcal F|_W\longrightarrow0
$$
is exact at $\mathcal F|_W$ and at every free term except the leftmost one. No exactness at the leftmost free term and no global analytic free resolution are asserted.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $N\ge0$, let $U$ be an open neighborhood
of $x\in\mathbb C^N$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a coherent analytic
$\mathcal O_U$-module. A coordinate polydisc centered at $x$ means a set
$$W=\{z\in\mathbb C^N:|z_j-x_j|<r_j\ (1\le j\le N)\},\qquad r_j>0,$$
contained in $U$. There is such a $W$ for which the following hold.

For every nonempty coordinate polydisc $D\subseteq W$ and every integer
$q>0$, ordinary derived-functor sheaf cohomology satisfies
$$H^q(D,\mathcal F|_D)=0.$$
On each such $D$, scalar sheaf cohomology of $\mathcal O_D$ is computed by the
global smooth Dolbeault complex. Here $\mathcal A_D^{0,q}$ is the sheaf of
smooth complex-valued differential forms of type $(0,q)$ and $\bar\partial$ is
the Dolbeault differential:
$$\Gamma(D,\mathcal A_D^{0,0})\xrightarrow{\bar\partial}\cdots \xrightarrow{\bar\partial}\Gamma(D,\mathcal A_D^{0,N}),$$
and in particular $H^q(D,\mathcal O_D)=0$ for $q>0$. The polydisc $W$ may be
chosen inside a neighborhood on which there is a partial finite-rank free resolution
$$\mathcal O_W^{p_\ell}\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow \mathcal O_W^{p_0}\longrightarrow\mathcal F|_W\longrightarrow0$$
that is exact at $\mathcal F|_W$ and at every free term except possibly the
leftmost one, with $\ell=2N+1>2N$. No exactness at the leftmost term and no
global free resolution are asserted.

For an integer $n\ge1$, **complex projective space** is the set of complex lines in $\mathbb C^{n+1}$ with the quotient topology
$$\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C):=(\mathbb C^{n+1}\setminus\{0\})/\mathbb C^\times,\qquad [z_0:\cdots:z_n]:=\mathbb C^\times(z_0,\ldots,z_n).$$
The quotient projection is continuous and surjective. Its restriction to the unit sphere $S^{2n+1}\subset\mathbb C^{n+1}$ is still surjective, so $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ is compact. It is Hausdorff: the map sending a nonzero vector $z$ to the orthogonal projection $zz^*/\lVert z\rVert^2$ is continuous and constant on each complex line, hence descends by the quotient topology to a continuous injection from $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ into the Hausdorff space of complex matrices. A continuous injection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism onto its image.

For open $V\subseteq\mathbb C^r$, a map $H:V\to\mathbb C^s$ is **holomorphic** if at every $a\in V$ there is a complex-linear map $A_a:\mathbb C^r\to\mathbb C^s$ such that $H(a+h)=H(a)+A_a h+R_a(h)$ with $\lVert R_a(h)\rVert/\lVert h\rVert\to0$ as $h\to0$, $h\ne0$. When $r=1$, this is equivalent to each component being holomorphic in the sense of [[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]], since a finite vector of scalar difference quotients converges exactly when each component does. A complex atlas consists of charts into $\mathbb C^n$ with holomorphic transitions in both directions.

For $j\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$ let $U_j:=\{[z_0:\cdots:z_n]:z_j\ne0\}$. These open sets cover projective space: their inverse images under the quotient projection are the open saturated sets where $z_j\ne0$. The **standard chart** is
$$\varphi_j:U_j\longrightarrow\mathbb C^n,\qquad [z_0:\cdots:z_n]\longmapsto (z_0/z_j,\ldots,\widehat{z_j/z_j},\ldots,z_n/z_j),$$
where the $j$th coordinate is omitted. It is well defined under rescaling. The coordinate-ratio map on the inverse image of $U_j$ is continuous and constant on each quotient fibre, so the quotient topology makes $\varphi_j$ continuous; its inverse inserts $1$ in the $j$th position and is continuous by composition with the quotient projection. Hence it is a homeomorphism. On $U_j\cap U_k$ the transition from the $j$th chart to the $k$th chart sends each coordinate $w_\ell=z_\ell/z_j$ ($\ell\ne j$) to $w_\ell/w_k$ for $\ell\ne k$, with the omitted $j$th coordinate equal to $1/w_k$. To check holomorphy at $a$ with $a_k\ne0$, set $a_j=1$ and $h_j=0$ for the omitted source coordinate. Each target coordinate has the expansion $(a_\ell+h_\ell)/(a_k+h_k)=a_\ell/a_k+h_\ell/a_k-a_\ell h_k/a_k^2+O(\lVert h\rVert^2)$ for $\ell\ne k$. The linear term is complex-linear, and the remainder estimate follows by expanding the reciprocal at the nonzero $a_k$. The inverse transition has the same form, so both are holomorphic. Thus these charts make $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ a complex manifold of complex dimension $n$ and a topological manifold of real dimension $2n$ in the sense of [[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]]. The finite chart cover by second-countable copies of $\mathbb C^n$ gives a countable base. Its rational transition functions have smooth real coordinate expressions on their domains, so the atlas also defines the smooth structure in the sense of [[def-smooth-manifold]]. The space is path-connected: distinct lines represented by $u,v$ give the path $t\mapsto[(1-t)u+tv]$, whose vector never vanishes because $u,v$ are linearly independent; equal lines give a constant path. In particular, $\mathbb P^1(\mathbb C)$ is a Riemann surface in the sense of [[def-riemann-surface-and-holomorphic-atlas]].

A map $F:X\to\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ from a Riemann surface is **holomorphic** when it is continuous and every component of each chart expression $\varphi_j\circ F$, written in a local coordinate of $X$, is holomorphic on the open set $F^{-1}(U_j)$. On an overlap, the new components are $f_\ell/f_k$ and $1/f_k$, where the $f_\ell$ are the old components and $f_k\ne0$. The scalar quotient rule gives their holomorphy ([[thm-algebra-of-complex-derivatives]]), so it suffices to check one target chart locally. Changing the source coordinate composes each scalar component with a one-variable holomorphic chart transition, where [[thm-chain-rule-for-complex-derivatives]] applies ([[def-holomorphic-and-meromorphic-map-of-riemann-surfaces]]). A **projective line** is the image in $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ of a two-dimensional complex subspace of $\mathbb C^{n+1}$. Every invertible linear map of $\mathbb C^{n+1}$ induces a holomorphic projective linear transformation: in source and target standard charts its coordinates are ratios of affine-linear functions with nonzero denominator, and the same reciprocal expansion gives a complex-linear derivative; these transformations act transitively on $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$.

Fix a natural number $m\ge1$. **Complex $m$-space** $\mathbb C^m$ is the set of
functions $m\to\mathbb C$, so a point $z$ has coordinates $z_k$ for $k<m$,
indexed from $0$ exactly as $\mathbb R^n$ is in this library. With coordinatewise
addition and multiplication by complex scalars it is a vector space over the
field $\mathbb C$ ([[def-vector-space]], [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]),
with the standard basis $e_0,\dots,e_{m-1}$ of [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]].

**The coordinate identification.** Writing $z_k=x_k+iy_k$ with $x_k,y_k$ real
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define

$$\Phi:\mathbb C^m\to\mathbb R^{2m},\qquad \Phi(z)=(x_0,y_0,x_1,y_1,\dots,x_{m-1},y_{m-1}).$$

The interleaved ordering is the one used throughout this page; the ordering that
groups all real parts before all imaginary parts is a **different** bijection,
and nothing below is stated for it. $\Phi$ is a bijection and is
$\mathbb R$-linear.

**Norms agree.** Put $\lVert z\rVert:=\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|z_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$. Since
$|z_k|^2=x_k^2+y_k^2$, this is the Euclidean norm $\lVert\Phi(z)\rVert_2$ of
[[def-p-norms-on-rn]] and [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and it is a norm on
the real vector space underlying $\mathbb C^m$ in the sense of
[[def-norm-and-normed-space]]. Consequently
$\lVert z-w\rVert=\lVert\Phi(z)-\Phi(w)\rVert_2$, so the metric of
$\mathbb C^m$, its balls ([[def-metric-ball]]), its open sets, its convergent
sequences, its Cauchy sequences and its continuous maps are **verbatim** those of
$\mathbb R^{2m}$ under $\Phi$. In particular convergence and continuity are
coordinatewise ([[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]],
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]), $\mathbb C^m$ is complete
([[thm-componentwise-convergence-and-completeness]]), and a subset of
$\mathbb C^m$ is compact exactly when it is closed and bounded
([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

**At $m=1$ this is the published plane dictionary.** For $m=1$ the map $\Phi$ is
the bijection of [[rem-complex-plane-euclidean-dictionary]] and every clause
above reduces to a clause recorded there. Openness, connectedness and real total
differentiability on $\mathbb C^m$ are always read through $\Phi$, exactly as
that remark reads them through its own identification.

**What $\Phi$ does not carry.** $\Phi$ respects the additive and the real scalar
structure but not multiplication by $i$ in any way visible to a general
$\mathbb R$-linear map of $\mathbb R^{2m}$: an $\mathbb R$-linear map of
$\mathbb C^m$ need not be $\mathbb C$-linear. That distinction is the whole
content of the criterion the page proves next, and it is why "linear" is always
qualified below.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty. The following are equivalent.

1. $A$ is compact.
2. $A$ is closed and bounded.
3. $A$ is pseudocompact.
4. Every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $A$.

This theorem is a ZF statement. The nonemptiness hypothesis is necessary for condition 4, because the empty image has neither a maximum nor a minimum.

Let $(X,\mathcal O_X)$ be a ringed space, so $X$ is a topological space and $\mathcal O_X$ is a sheaf of commutative rings. An $\mathcal O_X$-module sheaf $\mathcal F$ is **locally of finite type** if for every $x\in X$ there are an open neighborhood $U$ of $x$, a finite integer $r\ge0$, and sections $s_1,\ldots,s_r\in\mathcal F(U)$ such that their germs generate $\mathcal F_y$ as an $\mathcal O_{X,y}$-module for every $y\in U$.

For an open $V\subseteq X$, a finite integer $p\ge0$, and an $\mathcal O_X$-module morphism $\phi:\mathcal O_V^{\oplus p}\to\mathcal F|_V$, its **relation sheaf** is the kernel sheaf $\ker\phi$. The module sheaf $\mathcal F$ is **coherent** if it is locally of finite type and, for every such $V$, $p$, and $\phi$, the relation sheaf $\ker\phi$ is locally of finite type. Here $\mathcal O_V^{\oplus0}$ is the zero module sheaf.

In particular, for a finite tuple $f_1,\ldots,f_p\in\mathcal O_X(U)$, its holomorphic relation sheaf is the kernel of the morphism $\mathcal O_U^{\oplus p}\to\mathcal O_U$ that sends $(a_1,\ldots,a_p)$ to $\sum_{j=1}^p a_jf_j$. The structure sheaf is coherent when it is coherent as a module over itself. If $M$ is a complex manifold, an **analytic coherent module on $M$** means a coherent module sheaf over its sheaf $\mathcal O_M$ of holomorphic functions.

Assume full AC. Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional complex manifold, let $\mathcal F$ be a coherent analytic $\mathcal O_M$-module, and let $V$ be a nonempty open subset of one holomorphic chart on which a finite presentation $\mathcal O_V^{p_1}\to\mathcal O_V^{p_0}\xrightarrow{\pi}\mathcal F|_V\to0$ is fixed. Assume that the induced section map $\Gamma(V,\mathcal O_V^{p_0})\to\Gamma(V,\mathcal F)$ is surjective. Then its quotient topology from compact-convergence on $\mathcal O(V)^{p_0}$ is a Fréchet topology. If two such presentations are locally defined on a common cover and both section maps are surjective, their quotient topologies agree; the compatible-family topology on sections over any open set admitting a countable cover by such presentation neighborhoods is also Fréchet and independent of the chosen chart cover and presentations.

Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional complex manifold, let $\mathcal O_M$ be its sheaf of holomorphic functions, and let $\mathcal F$ be a coherent $\mathcal O_M$-module sheaf. On an open set $V$ contained in a coordinate chart and in a neighborhood with a finite presentation $\mathcal O_V^{p_1}\to\mathcal O_V^{p_0}\xrightarrow{\pi}\mathcal F|_V\to0$, where $p_0,p_1$ are finite nonnegative ranks, require that the section map $\Gamma(V,\mathcal O_V^{p_0})\to\Gamma(V,\mathcal F)$ is surjective. Give $\mathcal O(V)^{p_0}$ the compact-convergence topology generated by the seminorms $f\mapsto\sup_{z\in K}\lVert f(z)\rVert$ for compact $K\subset V$, and give $\Gamma(V,\mathcal F)$ the quotient topology induced by that surjection. On any open subset covered by countably many such sets, use the topology of the closed subspace of the product of their local section spaces consisting of compatible families. For a finite ordered open cover $\mathcal U=(U_i)$ whose nonempty finite intersections have these section topologies, give each Čech cochain space

$$C^q(\mathcal U,\mathcal F):=\prod_{i_0<\cdots<i_q}\Gamma(U_{i_0}\cap\cdots\cap U_{i_q},\mathcal F),\qquad (\delta c)_{i_0\cdots i_{q+1}}=\sum_{\nu=0}^{q+1}(-1)^\nu c_{i_0\cdots\widehat{i_\nu}\cdots i_{q+1}}\big|_{U_{i_0}\cap\cdots\cap U_{i_{q+1}}}.$$

the finite-product topology, give its cocycle space the subspace topology, and give the quotient of cocycles by coboundaries the Čech quotient topology. The accompanying Fréchet-quotient lemma proves local chart and presentation independence; the compact projective-space finiteness theorem proves independence of its admissible finite acyclic cover topology.

Assume full AC and the local Oka interface stated below. Let $r\ge1$, let $M$ be a complex manifold of complex dimension $r$, and let $V$ be an open subset of $M$ on which a coherent analytic module $\mathcal F$ is defined. Let $D_1,\ldots,D_s$ be relatively compact coordinate polydiscs in $M$ with nonempty intersection $V=\bigcap_{i=1}^sD_i$. Suppose that for one index $i_0$, a neighborhood of $\overline{D_{i_0}}$ in its chart lies in the domain of $\mathcal F$ and carries an exact partial finite-rank free resolution of $\mathcal F$ of length $2r$. Then $H^q(V,\mathcal F|_V)=0$ for every $q>0$. The result applies to a disconnected $V$ componentwise. The assumed local Oka interface is: under AC, on every finite-dimensional complex manifold $\mathcal O_M$ is coherent, coherent modules are closed under kernels, cokernels and finite extensions, and for each coherent $\mathcal F$, point $x$ and finite integer $\ell\ge0$, an exact partial finite-rank resolution $\mathcal O^{p_\ell}\to\cdots\to\mathcal O^{p_0}\to\mathcal F\to0$ exists on a chart neighborhood, exact at the module and all free terms except possibly the leftmost. No global free resolution is asserted.

Assume full AC. Let $m\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ be open, and let $\Omega'\subseteq\Omega$ be open with compact closure contained in $\Omega$. Let $\mathcal F$ be a coherent analytic module on a neighborhood of $\overline\Omega'$. Suppose it has a finite presentation by free sheaves on $\Omega$ and that the presentation section maps on both $\Omega$ and $\Omega'$ are surjective. Give the two section spaces the quotient topologies from compact-convergence on the finite free section spaces. Then the restriction map $\Gamma(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to\Gamma(\Omega',\mathcal F)$ is compact, meaning that it sends some neighborhood of zero to a set with compact closure.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $(E^\bullet,d)$ and $(F^\bullet,\delta)$ be cochain complexes of Fréchet spaces over $\mathbb C$, with continuous differentials, and let $\rho^\bullet:E^\bullet\to F^\bullet$ be a continuous cochain map. Fix $q\ge0$. If $\rho^q:E^q\to F^q$ is compact and the induced map $H^q(\rho^\bullet):H^q(E^\bullet)\to H^q(F^\bullet)$ is surjective, then $H^q(F^\bullet)$, with its cocycle-subspace and coboundary-quotient topology, is Hausdorff and finite-dimensional. Moreover, whenever a continuous cochain map between Fréchet complexes induces a surjection on $q$th cohomology, that cohomology map is open.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a
topological space, let $\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of abelian groups on $X$ and let
$\mathcal U=(U_i)_{i\in I}$ be an open cover of $X$ indexed by a linearly
ordered set which is $\mathcal F$-acyclic, that is, every nonempty finite
intersection of members of $\mathcal U$ satisfies
$H^q(W,\mathcal F|_W)=0$ for all $q>0$
([[def-acyclic-cover-for-sheaf]]). Then the canonical Čech-to-sheaf comparison
map
$$\varphi^p_{\mathcal U}:\check H^p(\mathcal U,\mathcal F)\longrightarrow H^p(X,\mathcal F)$$
of [[thm-cech-to-sheaf-cohomology-comparison]] is an isomorphism for every
$p\ge0$; it is natural in $\mathcal F$, compatible with refinement, and in
degree zero it is the identity of $\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)$ under the canonical
identifications of $\check H^0(\mathcal U,\mathcal F)$ and
$H^0(X,\mathcal F)$ with the global sections
([[thm-cech-to-sheaf-cohomology-comparison]],
[[def-cech-cohomology-open-cover]],
[[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a
topological space, let $\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of abelian groups on $X$ and let
$\mathcal U=(U_i)_{i\in I}$ be an open cover of $X$ indexed by a linearly
ordered set, with fixed-cover Čech cohomology
$\check H^\bullet(\mathcal U,\mathcal F)$
([[def-cech-cohomology-open-cover]]) and with sheaf cohomology
$H^\bullet(X,-)$ formed from the supplied injective resolution datum
([[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]). Let
$0\to\mathcal F\to G^\bullet$ be the Godement resolution
([[def-godement-resolution]]), let $D$ be the Čech–Godement double complex
$D^{p,q}=C^p(\mathcal U,G^q)$ and let
$$u:\Gamma(X,G^\bullet)\to\operatorname{Tot}D,\qquad w:C^\bullet(\mathcal U,\mathcal F)\to\operatorname{Tot}D$$
be the two cochain maps of [[lem-acyclic-rows-and-columns-of-cech-double-complex]],
where a global section is placed in the components $D^{0,q}$ as the family of
its restrictions to the members of $\mathcal U$ and a Čech cochain is placed in
the components $D^{p,0}$ through the morphism $\varepsilon:\mathcal F\to G^0$.
By that lemma $u$ is a quasi-isomorphism, and the Godement resolution computes
sheaf cohomology,
$$H^q(X,\mathcal F)\cong H^q\bigl(\Gamma(X,G^\bullet)\bigr)$$
naturally in $\mathcal F$ ([[thm-godement-resolution-flasque]]). The
**Čech-to-sheaf comparison map**
$$\varphi^p_{\mathcal U}:\check H^p(\mathcal U,\mathcal F)\longrightarrow H^p(X,\mathcal F)$$
is the composite $H^p(u)^{-1}\circ H^p(w)$ under these identifications. Then:

1. $\varphi^\bullet$ is natural in $\mathcal F$: for a morphism
$\phi:\mathcal F\to\mathcal G$ of abelian sheaves the square
$$\begin{matrix}\check H^p(\mathcal U,\mathcal F)&\xrightarrow{\ \varphi^p_{\mathcal U}(\mathcal F)\ }&H^p(X,\mathcal F)\\ \downarrow\scriptstyle{\check H^p(\mathcal U,\phi)}&&\downarrow\scriptstyle{H^p(X,\phi)}\\ \check H^p(\mathcal U,\mathcal G)&\xrightarrow{\ \varphi^p_{\mathcal U}(\mathcal G)\ }&H^p(X,\mathcal G)\end{matrix}$$
commutes for every $p\ge0$;
2. $\varphi^\bullet$ is compatible with refinement: for every refinement
function $c:J\to I$ from a cover $\mathcal V=(V_j)_{j\in J}$ to $\mathcal U$
with induced cochain map
$c^\sharp:C^\bullet(\mathcal U,\mathcal F)\to C^\bullet(\mathcal V,\mathcal F)$
([[def-refinement-open-cover]]) one has
$$\varphi^p_{\mathcal V}\circ H^p(c^\sharp)=\varphi^p_{\mathcal U}\qquad(p\ge0),$$
and by [[thm-refinement-map-independent-on-cohomology]] the left-hand side does
not depend on the choice of the refinement function $c$;
3. $\varphi^0_{\mathcal U}$ is the identity of $\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)$ under the
canonical identifications $\check H^0(\mathcal U,\mathcal F)\cong\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)$
([[lem-cech-h0-global-sections]]) and
$H^0(X,\mathcal F)\cong\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)$
([[thm-zero-sheaf-cohomology-global-sections]]).

Let $X$ be a topological space, let $\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of abelian groups
on $X$ ([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]]), and let
$\mathcal U=(U_i)_{i\in I}$ be a cover of $X$ by open subsets, indexed by a set
$I$ that is equipped with a linear order $<$.

For an integer $p\ge0$ define the **group of ordered $p$-cochains of
$\mathcal U$ with values in $\mathcal F$** by
$$C^p(\mathcal U,\mathcal F):=\prod_{i_0<\cdots<i_p} \mathcal F\bigl(U_{i_0}\cap\cdots\cap U_{i_p}\bigr),$$
the product of the section groups over all increasing $(p+1)$-tuples
$i_0<\cdots<i_p$ in $I$; write an element as $s=(s_{i_0\cdots i_p})$. For
$p<0$ put $C^p(\mathcal U,\mathcal F):=0$. When $I$ has no increasing
$(p+1)$-tuple the product is empty and $C^p(\mathcal U,\mathcal F)=0$; when an
intersection $U_{i_0}\cap\cdots\cap U_{i_p}$ is empty, the corresponding
factor is the one-element group $\mathcal F(\varnothing)=0$
([[lem-sheaf-section-over-empty-set-terminal]]).

The **Čech differential** $\delta^p:C^p(\mathcal U,\mathcal F)\to
C^{p+1}(\mathcal U,\mathcal F)$ is defined on an increasing $(p+2)$-tuple
$i_0<\cdots<i_{p+1}$ by
$$(\delta^p s)_{i_0\cdots i_{p+1}} =\sum_{j=0}^{p+1}(-1)^j\, s_{i_0\cdots\widehat{i_j}\cdots i_{p+1}} \Big|_{U_{i_0}\cap\cdots\cap U_{i_{p+1}}},$$
where $\widehat{i_j}$ means that the index $i_j$ is omitted and the restriction
is taken from $U_{i_0}\cap\cdots\widehat{U_{i_j}}\cdots\cap U_{i_{p+1}}$ to the
full intersection ([[def-section-restriction-and-global-section]]). For $p<0$
set $\delta^p:=0$. The maps $\delta^p$ are group homomorphisms, componentwise
sums of restrictions, so the data $(C^p(\mathcal U,\mathcal F),\delta^p)_{p\in
\mathbb Z}$ form a cochain complex of abelian groups; that $\delta^{p+1}\circ
\delta^p=0$ is proved in [[lem-cech-differential-squares-zero]]. The pair
$(\mathcal F,\mathcal U)$ being fixed, the construction is functorial in
$\mathcal F$: a morphism $\varphi:\mathcal F\to\mathcal G$ of abelian sheaves
induces componentwise maps $C^p(\mathcal U,\varphi)$ commuting with the
differentials.

Let $X$ be a topological space, $\mathcal F$ a sheaf of abelian groups on $X$
and $\mathcal U=(U_i)_{i\in I}$ an open cover indexed by a linearly ordered set
$I$, with ordered Čech cochains $C^p(\mathcal U,\mathcal F)$ as in
[[def-cech-cochain-complex-open-cover]]. Then for every $p\in\mathbb Z$
$$\delta^{p+1}\circ\delta^p=0,$$
so that $\bigl(C^\bullet(\mathcal U,\mathcal F),\delta^\bullet\bigr)$ is a
cochain complex.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let
$$0\to\mathcal F'\to\mathcal F\to\mathcal F''\to0$$
be a short exact sequence of abelian sheaves on a topological space $X$, and let
$H^q(X,-)$ be sheaf cohomology computed from the supplied functorial injective
resolution datum $I$ on $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$
([[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]). Then there is a natural long
exact sequence
$$\cdots\to H^q(X,\mathcal F')\to H^q(X,\mathcal F)\to H^q(X,\mathcal F'')\xrightarrow{\partial^q}H^{q+1}(X,\mathcal F')\to H^{q+1}(X,\mathcal F)\to\cdots,$$
natural in the short exact sequence and independent of the choice of injective
resolutions used to assemble it.

The derived categories and right derived functor here are taken under the
standing smallness or supplied cofinal-denominator hypothesis of
[[def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category]].

derivations.claim: If $r=0$, $P^0(\mathbb C)$ is a point and $\mathcal O_{P^0}=\mathbb C$. Coherence makes its module of global sections finitely generated over $\mathbb C$, hence finite-dimensional. Sheaves on a point are abelian groups and global sections is the identity functor, so positive right-derived global sections vanish. Every finite-presentation quotient topology on this finite-dimensional space is Hausdorff; finite-dimensional complex vector spaces have a unique Hausdorff locally convex topology, so the cover/presentation topology is independent.

Suppose $1\le r\le3$ and fix $x\in P^r$. Apply [A1] to $\mathcal F$ at $x$ with length $2r$ to obtain a chart neighborhood $W_0$ with a partial free resolution. Its first relation kernel $K_0$ is coherent by [A1]. Apply [A1] again to $K_0$ at $x$ with length $2r$, and choose a neighborhood $W_1\subseteq W_0$ on which that kernel resolution is defined. Apply [A2] to $\mathcal F$ at $x$ to obtain a polydisc neighborhood $W_2$. Choose concentric coordinate polydiscs $D'_x\Subset D_x$ with $\overline{D_x}\subseteq W_1\cap W_2$. Then $D'_x$ is a neighborhood of $x$.

For any finite family of centers $x_1,\ldots,x_s$ with nested pairs $D'_{x_i}\Subset D_{x_i}$ as in the local construction above and with the $D'_{x_i}$ covering $P^r$, put $U_i=D_{x_i}$ and $U'_i=D'_{x_i}$. Conditional on such a choice, the refinement from $\mathcal U=(U_i)$ to $\mathcal U'=(U'_i)$ uses the same index set and sends each index $i$ to itself. In every degree its cochain map is componentwise restriction $\Gamma(U_I,\mathcal F)\to\Gamma(U'_I,\mathcal F)$. It commutes with the Čech differential because restriction of sections commutes with each term of the alternating sum [F8].

The sets $D'_x$ cover $P^r$. Compactness [F1] gives finitely many centers $x_1,\ldots,x_s$ whose smaller polydiscs still cover; set $U_i=D_{x_i}$ and $U'_i=D'_{x_i}$. Each singleton $U_i$ and $U'_i$ is $\mathcal F$-acyclic by [A2]. For every nonempty finite intersection of at least two of the $U_i$, the intersection lemma [F4] applies using the length-$2r$ resolution of $\mathcal F$ on the closure of any participating $U_i$. It also applies to the corresponding intersections of the $U'_i$, since their closures lie inside those same resolution neighborhoods. Thus both finite covers are acyclic for $\mathcal F$.

On any nonempty intersection $V=U_I$ or $V=U'_I$, use the first presentation of $\mathcal F$ from a chosen participating $U_{i_0}$. Its relation kernel is $K_0|_V$, and the same local Oka construction in step 1.2 gives a length-$2r$ resolution of $K_0$ on a neighborhood of $\overline{U_{i_0}}$. Applying [F4] to $K_0$ on $V$ gives $H^1(V,K_0)=0$. The long exact sequence of $0\to K_0\to\mathcal O_V^{p_0}\to\mathcal F|_V\to0$ then makes the section map $\Gamma(V,\mathcal O_V^{p_0})\to\Gamma(V,\mathcal F)$ surjective. Therefore [F3] supplies the required Fréchet section and Čech topologies on both covers.

For every index set $I$, $\overline{U'_I}\subseteq\bigcap_{i\in I}\overline{U'_i}\subseteq U_I$, and this closure is compact because it is a closed subset of the finite intersection of the compact sets $\overline{U'_i}$. Every nonzero component of the cochain map in step 1.3 is therefore a restriction with relatively compact target, hence compact by [F5]. For the finitely many components in a fixed degree, choose in each source a zero-neighborhood whose restriction has compact closure; their finite product is a zero-neighborhood and the product of those compact closures is compact. Thus the full cochain map in that degree is compact.

Both covers in step 2.1 are acyclic for $\mathcal F$. By [F7], the induced map on Čech cohomology is the identity comparison through $H^q(P^r,\mathcal F)$, hence an isomorphism in every degree. In particular it is surjective.

Each Čech cochain space is a finite product of Fréchet section spaces by [F3], and restrictions are continuous, so the two Čech cochain complexes are Fréchet complexes. By steps 3.2–3.3, their cochain map is compact in degree $q$ and surjective on degree-$q$ cohomology. Apply [F6] to conclude that $H^q(C^\bullet(\mathcal U',\mathcal F))$ is Hausdorff and finite-dimensional. The Leray comparison [F7] transfers both conclusions to $H^q(P^r,\mathcal F)$. If $q$ is at least the number of cover members, the Čech cochain space is zero and the conclusion is immediate as well.

To compare two finite admissible covers, retain the given presentation $\pi_I$ on every nonempty intersection $U_I$ of either parent cover, and write $K_I=\ker\pi_I$; there are only finitely many such coherent kernels by [A1]. First shrink each parent cover to open sets $B_i$ with $\overline{B_i}\subset U_i$, still covering $P^r$: at every point choose a coordinate polydisc with compact closure in some parent member, take a finite subcover by compactness [F1], and for each parent member take the union of its finitely many assigned polydiscs. Do this for both parent covers. At a point $x$, repeat step 1.2 for $\mathcal F$ and its new presentation kernel. In addition, for every parent intersection $U_I$ containing $x$, use [A1] to choose a length-$2r$ resolution neighborhood of its particular kernel $K_I$. Intersect these finitely many neighborhoods. Choose nested polydiscs $D'_x\Subset D_x$ whose closures lie in this intersection and in one selected $B_i$ from each parent cover. Also choose $\overline{D_x}$ disjoint from every $\overline{B_j}$ whose parent $U_j$ does not contain $x$; those are finitely many closed sets missing $x$. Compactness gives a finite cover $\mathcal W$ by some of the $D'_x$, with the selected parent assignments. As in steps 1.2, 2.1 and 3.1, its intersections are $\mathcal F$-acyclic and have surjective finite-presentation section maps. Now take a nonempty refined intersection $T=D'_{x_0}\cap\cdots\cap D'_{x_k}$ and one parent cover. Let $I$ be its distinct assigned parent indices. Since $D'_{x_0}$ meets each selected $B_i$, the avoidance condition implies $x_0\in U_i$ for every $i\in I$. Hence the closure of $D'_{x_0}$ lies inside a resolution neighborhood for this very $K_I$. Applying [F4] to $K_I$ on $T$ gives $H^1(T,K_I)=0$, so [F9] proves surjectivity of the section map of the SAME parent presentation $\pi_I|_T$. Its section map on $U_I$ is surjective by parent admissibility. Moreover $\overline T$ is compact in $U_I$, since each refined polydisc has compact closure in its assigned parent. Thus [F5] applies to $\Gamma(U_I,\mathcal F)\to\Gamma(T,\mathcal F)$ using that common presentation. By [F3], the resulting target quotient topology agrees with the chosen one on $T$. This works for both parent covers and all tuples; no newly chosen presentation is substituted for a parent presentation without proving its section surjectivity.

For either parent cover, the standard refinement cochain map to $\mathcal W$ sends a component to its restriction with the sign of the permutation that sorts the parent indices, and sends it to zero when two parent indices repeat. The alternating formula [F8] shows it is a cochain map: with distinct parents, deletion commutes with restriction and permutation signs; with a repeated parent, the two faces deleting that repeated pair cancel. Each nonzero component restriction is continuous by [F3] and compact by [F5]; its refined intersection has compact closure in the corresponding parent intersection by step 4.2. The covers are finite, so the finite-product argument of step 3.2 makes both cochain maps compact. Their induced cohomology maps are isomorphisms by [F7], hence surjective and open by [F6]; the maps themselves are continuous as cochain maps, so these bijections are topological isomorphisms. Therefore the two original Čech quotient topologies agree.

Assume full AC. For $0\le r\le3$, let $P^r(\mathbb C)$ be the space of complex lines in $\mathbb C^{r+1}$ with its usual complex-manifold structure, and let $\mathcal F$ be a coherent analytic module over its holomorphic structure sheaf. Write $H^q(P^r(\mathbb C),\mathcal F)$ for the $q$th right-derived global-sections group. Then every such group is finite-dimensional over $\mathbb C$ for every integer $q\ge0$.

For its topology, a coordinate polydisc means the image in a holomorphic chart of a product of open coordinate discs. Take any finite ordered cover $\mathcal U=(U_i)$ by relatively compact coordinate polydiscs such that each nonempty finite intersection $U_I$ has a finite presentation $\mathcal O_{U_I}^{p_1}\to\mathcal O_{U_I}^{p_0}\to\mathcal F|_{U_I}\to0$ whose global section map is surjective, and such that $H^q(U_I,\mathcal F|_{U_I})=0$ for every $q>0$. Give $\mathcal O(U_I)^{p_0}$ compact-convergence topology and $\Gamma(U_I,\mathcal F)$ the induced quotient topology. Set $C^k(\mathcal U,\mathcal F)=\prod_{i_0<\cdots<i_k}\Gamma(U_{i_0}\cap\cdots\cap U_{i_k},\mathcal F)$ with finite-product topology and differential
$$
(\delta c)_{i_0\cdots i_{k+1}}=\sum_{\nu=0}^{k+1}(-1)^\nu c_{i_0\cdots\widehat{i_\nu}\cdots i_{k+1}}\big|_{U_{i_0}\cap\cdots\cap U_{i_{k+1}}}.
$$
Give the cocycle space its subspace topology and its quotient by coboundaries the Čech quotient topology. These cohomology groups are Hausdorff in that topology, which is independent of the chosen finite cover and local presentations.

Let $X$ be a topological space, let $x\in X$, and let $A$ be an abelian group.
The **skyscraper sheaf at $x$ with value $A$** is the sheaf
$$
i_{x,*}A
$$
defined on an open set $V \subseteq X$ by
$$(i_{x,*}A)(V)= \begin{cases} A,& x\in V,\\ 0,& x\notin V. \end{cases}$$
If $V' \subseteq V$ and both opens contain $x$, the restriction map is the
identity on $A$. If $x\notin V'$, the restriction map to $0$ is the unique zero
homomorphism.

Thus a skyscraper sheaf has the value $A$ precisely on opens that meet the
chosen point.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, let $X$ be a topological space and let
$\mathcal F$ be a flasque sheaf of abelian groups on $X$
([[def-flasque-sheaf]]). Then for every open subspace $U\subseteq X$ and every
integer $q>0$,
$$H^q(U,\mathcal F|_U)=0,$$
where $H^q(U,-)$ denotes sheaf cohomology on the space $U$
([[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]) computed with the global
sections functor of $U$, and $\mathcal F|_U$ is the restriction of $\mathcal F$
to $U$. Equivalently, every restriction $\mathcal F|_U$ is $\Gamma$-acyclic
([[def-acyclic-sheaf-global-sections]]).

Let $\mathcal F$ be a presheaf on a topological space $X$, and let $x\in X$.

The **neighbourhood category of $x$** is the full subcategory
$$\mathcal N_x\subseteq \operatorname{Open}(X)$$
whose objects are the open neighbourhoods of $x$. Its opposite category is
filtered in the sense of
[[def-filtered-category-and-filtered-colimit]]: it is nonempty because $X$
itself is a neighbourhood of $x$, and for neighbourhoods $U,V$ the
intersection $U\cap V$ is again a neighbourhood of $x$ with arrows
$$U\longrightarrow U\cap V,\qquad V\longrightarrow U\cap V$$
in the opposite category.

Because $\mathcal F$ is contravariant, its restriction to the neighbourhood
category determines a covariant diagram on that opposite category. The
**stalk** of $\mathcal F$ at $x$ is the filtered colimit
$$\mathcal F_x:=\varinjlim_{\mathcal N_x^{\operatorname{op}}}\mathcal F(U).$$

Concretely, $\mathcal F_x$ may be described as equivalence classes of pairs
$(U,s)$ with $U$ an open neighbourhood of $x$ and
$s\in\mathcal F(U)$, where $(U,s)\sim(V,t)$ when $s$ and $t$ agree on some
smaller open neighbourhood of $x$. The next lemma verifies that this is an
equivalence relation.

Let $m\ge1$. A **chart** on a topological space $X$ is a homeomorphism
$\varphi:U\to\varphi(U)$ from an open set $U\subseteq X$ onto an open subset of
$\mathbb C^m$ with its usual topology ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]);
two charts $\varphi,\psi$ are **holomorphically compatible** when the
transition maps $\psi\circ\varphi^{-1}$ and $\varphi\circ\psi^{-1}$ are
holomorphic on the open sets where they are defined
([[def-holomorphic-function-in-several-complex-variables]]). A **holomorphic
atlas** is a family of pairwise compatible charts whose domains cover $X$. A
**complex manifold of dimension $m$** is a nonempty Hausdorff
([[def-hausdorff-space]]) second-countable ([[def-second-countable-space]])
topological space carrying a holomorphic atlas; the same maximal-atlas argument
as for [[def-riemann-surface-and-holomorphic-atlas]] applies verbatim with
$\mathbb C^m$ in place of $\mathbb C$: the union of a holomorphic atlas with all
charts compatible with it is again a holomorphic atlas, so one passes to the
unique maximal atlas and calls its members holomorphic charts. Each chart is a
homeomorphism onto an open subset of $\mathbb C^m\cong\mathbb R^{2m}$, so $X$ is
a topological manifold without boundary of real dimension $2m$
([[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]]), and for connected $X$ the case
$m=1$ recovers Riemann surfaces ([[def-riemann-surface-and-holomorphic-atlas]]).

A **holomorphic map** $f:X\to Y$ between complex manifolds is a continuous map
whose expression in every pair of holomorphic charts is holomorphic
([[def-holomorphic-map-and-complex-jacobian]]); equivalently, for every open
$V\subseteq Y$ and every holomorphic function $h$ on $V$, the function
$h\circ f$ is holomorphic on $f^{-1}(V)$. The forward implication is the
holomorphic chain rule; conversely apply this condition to the coordinate
functions of a chart on $Y$.

**Induced smooth structure and complex structure.** Holomorphic functions on
open subsets of $\mathbb C^m$ are smooth
([[cor-holomorphic-functions-in-several-variables-are-smooth]]), so every
holomorphic atlas is a smooth atlas ([[def-smooth-atlas]]) and $X$ is a smooth
manifold of real dimension $2m$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]]) whose smooth charts
include the holomorphic ones. In holomorphic coordinates
$z_k=x_k+iy_k$ the **complex structure** is the endomorphism field $J$ of the
tangent bundle determined by $J\partial_{x_k}=\partial_{y_k}$ and
$J\partial_{y_k}=-\partial_{x_k}$; it satisfies $J^2=-\mathrm{id}$ and is
independent of the holomorphic chart, because a holomorphic transition map has
complex-linear differential ([[def-holomorphic-map-and-complex-jacobian]],
[[thm-chain-rule-for-holomorphic-maps-in-several-variables]]) and complex-linear
maps intertwine the two coordinate definitions of multiplication by $i$. A
**Hermitian metric** on $X$ is a Riemannian metric $g$
([[def-riemannian-metric-and-riemannian-manifold]]) satisfying
$g(Jv,Jw)=g(v,w)$ for all tangent vectors $v,w$; its Riemannian volume density
is written $\mu_g$ ([[def-riemannian-volume-density]]). The complex structure
makes each tangent space a complex vector space, so the tangent bundle is a
smooth complex vector bundle in the sense of
[[def-complex-linear-and-compatible-bundle-connections]].

**Holomorphic vector bundles and Hermitian bundle metrics.** A **holomorphic
vector bundle of rank $r$** on $X$ is a smooth complex vector bundle
$\pi:E\to X$ of rank $r$
([[def-smooth-vector-bundle-rank-fibre-and-trivial-bundle]],
[[def-complex-linear-and-compatible-bundle-connections]]) together with an open
cover $(V_\alpha)$ of $X$ and smooth local trivializations
$\theta_\alpha:E|_{V_\alpha}\to V_\alpha\times\mathbb C^r$ whose transition
matrices $g_{\alpha\beta}:V_\alpha\cap V_\beta\to\mathrm{GL}_r(\mathbb C)$,
defined by $\theta_\alpha\theta_\beta^{-1}(p,v)=(p,g_{\alpha\beta}(p)v)$, are
holomorphic. A **holomorphic frame** over an open set $V$ is a smooth
complex-linear trivialization whose transition matrices with the supplied
trivializations are holomorphic on every overlap. Changing holomorphic frame multiplies a local section by a
holomorphic matrix, hence a smooth local section is **holomorphic** exactly when
its representatives in holomorphic frames are holomorphic functions. A
**Hermitian metric** $h$ on $E$ is a smooth bundle metric
([[def-smooth-bundle-metric]]) whose fibre pairings are positive definite
Hermitian forms, linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the
second; the condition is frame-independent because the gauge freedom is
conjugation by a pointwise invertible matrix. Smooth sections are
$\Gamma(E)$ ([[def-smooth-section-local-section-and-support]]).

Let $\mathcal F$ be a presheaf on a topological space $X$. We say that
$\mathcal F$ is a **sheaf** if for every open set $U \subseteq X$ and every
open cover $U=\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i$, including the empty cover of
$\varnothing$, the following two conditions hold.

**Locality.** If $s,t\in\mathcal F(U)$ satisfy
$$s|_{U_i}=t|_{U_i}\qquad\text{for all }i\in I,$$
then $s=t$.

**Gluing.** If sections $s_i\in\mathcal F(U_i)$ satisfy
$$s_i|_{U_i\cap U_j}=s_j|_{U_i\cap U_j}\qquad\text{for all }i,j\in I,$$
then there exists $s\in\mathcal F(U)$ such that
$$s|_{U_i}=s_i\qquad\text{for all }i\in I.$$

By locality, such a section $s$ is automatically unique. Thus a sheaf is
exactly a presheaf whose compatible local sections glue uniquely.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix a topological space $X$, let
$$\Gamma(X,-):\mathrm{Ab}(X)\to\mathbf{Ab}$$
be the additive left exact global-sections functor
([[def-global-sections-functor-sheaves]]), and let $I$ be the supplied
functorial injective resolution datum on $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ of
[[thm-abelian-sheaves-have-enough-injectives]]: it assigns to every abelian
sheaf $\mathcal F$ one specific injective resolution
$0\to\mathcal F\to I^\bullet(\mathcal F)$
([[def-right-derived-object-relative-to-injective-resolution-data]]).

For every $q\ge0$ and every abelian sheaf $\mathcal F$ on $X$ define the
**$q$-th sheaf cohomology group of $\mathcal F$** to be the right derived
object of $\Gamma(X,-)$ relative to $I$:
$$H^q(X,\mathcal F):=R_I^q\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)=H^q\bigl(\Gamma(X,I^\bullet(\mathcal F)_{\mathrm{del}})\bigr),$$
the cohomology object of the complex
$\Gamma(X,I^0(\mathcal F))\to\Gamma(X,I^1(\mathcal F))\to\cdots$ of abelian
groups obtained from the deleted resolution
([[def-deleted-resolution]], [[def-cohomology-object-of-a-cochain-complex]]).
We also set $H^q(X,\mathcal F):=0$ for $q<0$.

Because $I$ is a fixed supplied datum, the group $H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ is a
specific group for each pair $(X,\mathcal F)$, and for a morphism
$\varphi:\mathcal F\to\mathcal G$ of abelian sheaves we write
$H^q(X,\varphi):=R_I^q\Gamma(X,\varphi)$ for the induced map; it is the map on
cohomology induced by $\Gamma(X,-)$ applied to the cochain maps supplied with
the datum, and it is additive in $\varphi$.

If $J$ is another supplied injective resolution datum on $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ then
$R_I^q\Gamma(X,-)$ and $R_J^q\Gamma(X,-)$ are naturally isomorphic, so the
$H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ computed from $J$ agree with the ones above up to a
canonical natural isomorphism; the Axiom of Dependent Choice needed for that
comparison follows from AC
([[thm-right-derived-functors-from-two-supplied-injective-resolution-data-are-naturally-isomorphic]],
[[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]). The notation
$H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ therefore does not depend on the datum used, up to this
canonical isomorphism, and we call $q$ the **cohomological degree**.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, let $X$ be a topological space and let
$\mathcal F$ be a flasque sheaf of abelian groups on $X$
([[def-flasque-sheaf]]). Then for every open subspace $U\subseteq X$ and every
integer $q>0$,
$$H^q(U,\mathcal F|_U)=0,$$
where $H^q(U,-)$ denotes sheaf cohomology on the space $U$
([[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]) computed with the global
sections functor of $U$, and $\mathcal F|_U$ is the restriction of $\mathcal F$
to $U$. Equivalently, every restriction $\mathcal F|_U$ is $\Gamma$-acyclic
([[def-acyclic-sheaf-global-sections]]).

derivations.claim: By [F1], the cohomology groups in the Statement are finite-dimensional under the stated compactness and coherence assumptions. If $S=\varnothing$, [F4] makes $\mathcal F=0$, so all claims hold with $\ell=0$. Suppose $S\ne\varnothing$. Since $S$ is finite and $P^r$ is Hausdorff, choose pairwise disjoint open neighborhoods $V_x$ of its points, one for each $x\in S$ by [F5]. On $V_x\setminus\{x\}$ every stalk of $\mathcal F$ vanishes by the definition of $S$, so the restriction there is the zero sheaf by [F4].

For each $x\in S$, the germ map from $\mathcal F|_{V_x}$ to the skyscraper sheaf $i_{x,*}\mathcal F_x$ is an isomorphism. It is injective on sections because a section with zero germ at $x$ and zero stalk at every other point has zero germ everywhere, hence is zero by the uniqueness clause [F6]. It is surjective on sections over an open $W\subseteq V_x$ containing $x$: represent a desired germ by a section on a smaller neighborhood of $x$, restrict to the punctured overlap where $\mathcal F$ is zero, and glue that section to zero on $W\setminus\{x\}$ using [F6]. For $W$ not containing $x$, both section groups are zero.

The open complement $P^r\setminus S$ has zero restriction of $\mathcal F$, and the neighborhoods $V_x$ are pairwise disjoint. The local isomorphisms of step 2.1 therefore glue to a sheaf isomorphism $\mathcal F\cong\bigoplus_{x\in S}i_{x,*}\mathcal F_x$, where the sum is finite. Each skyscraper is flasque by [F2], since every restriction is either the identity or the map onto $0$; hence their finite direct sum is flasque. By [F3] and the ambient AC [A1], $H^q(P^r,\mathcal F)=0$ for $q>0$.

Taking global sections of the finite direct-sum decomposition in step 3.1 and using [F7] gives $H^0(P^r,\mathcal F)=\Gamma(P^r,\mathcal F)\cong\bigoplus_{x\in S}\mathcal F_x$. Its dimension is the finite sum $\ell$ from the Statement.
